prompt:
Add a `heading_offset` option to `markdown.Markdown` (and `markdown.markdown`): a whole number from 0 to 5, default 0, that shifts the level of every heading Markdown produces by that many (an `h1` becomes an `h2` with 1), never beyond `h6`. Any other value raises `ValueError`.
- It applies to hash and underline headings, and to headings from extensions such as `md_in_html`.
- The `toc` extension sees the shifted levels (its tokens and `toc_depth`).
- The command line gets `--heading-offset N`.

Work on your own; nobody will answer questions. When you finish, report: status `done` if you did the task, `not_found` if something the task names does not exist, `blocked` if you could not do it; `answer` holds any answer the task asks for (otherwise one short sentence); `changed` lists the files you changed.

report.answer: I added `heading_offset`, a whole number from 0 to 5 (default 0). Any other value raises `ValueError`, and that includes `True` and `1.0`. On the command line, `--heading-offset N` gives a usage error if N is outside 0–5. The shift is done by a new tree processor (priority 5.5) that runs just before `toc`. So it covers hash and underline headings, headings inside `md_in_html` blocks, and headings any extension adds to the tree. `toc`'s tokens and `toc_depth` see the shifted levels, and its own `baselevel` stacks on top of the offset. Headings written as plain raw HTML are passed through unchanged. One side effect: an `<hN markdown="1">` element in `md_in_html` is shifted too, matching how `toc` already treats it. Tests (including new ones in `test_heading_offset.py`), docs and a changelog entry are added, and the full test suite passes.
